1.open: Think of a time you started something new, like a job, a school, or a move. What was the first week like?
questions: The LORD begins with "Moses My servant is dead" (v. 2). Why might God say that so bluntly before giving Joshua his task?
Joshua had been Moses' assistant for years before this moment. What does that say about how people get ready for big responsibilities?
God says, "As I was with Moses, so will I be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you" (v. 5). When have you needed to hear that someone would stay with you?
Three times in this chapter Joshua is told to be strong and courageous (vv. 6, 7, 9). Why do you think God keeps repeating it? What does that suggest about how Joshua felt?
Verse 8 says, "This Book of the Law must not depart from your mouth; meditate on it day and night." What would it look like for you to keep God's word close in an ordinary week?

God gives Joshua land that other peoples already lived in, and Christians read that differently. Some see real divine judgment, others a national story told in the war language of its time. How do you feel when you read this part of the Bible?
Joshua reminds the eastern tribes to help their brothers "until the LORD gives them rest" (v. 15). Who in your life is still waiting for rest, and how could you help carry some of their load?
If you are honest, where do you feel more afraid or discouraged than strong right now? What would it mean to hear "the LORD your God is with you wherever you go" there (v. 9)?
1.life: Pick one person who is in a hard or unsettled season and do one concrete thing for them this week, such as a meal, a call, or an hour of help. Then, when you feel afraid, say verse 9 out loud.
1.prayer: Thank God that he goes with us into places we have never been. Ask for courage for anyone in the group facing something new or frightening.
1.tip: The land and war language in this chapter can unsettle people. Say plainly that Christians understand it differently, give a minute for honest reactions, and then steer back to what the chapter says about God's presence and courage. Don't try to settle it tonight.

2.open: Have you ever helped someone out of a tight spot, or been helped by someone you did not expect?
questions: The spies end up at the house of "a prostitute named Rahab" (v. 1). What do you notice about the kind of person God's story runs through here?
Rahab hides the men on her roof "among the stalks of flax" (v. 6) and sends the king's men the wrong way. What do you think she risked by doing this?
Rahab says, "I know that the LORD has given you this land" (v. 9). What had she heard, and how did it lead her to that conclusion?

In verse 11 she says, "the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below." What do you think it took for an outsider to say that? What has made God seem real or believable to you, or what has made it hard?
Rahab asks the spies to "show kindness to my family, because I showed kindness to you" (v. 12). Why might she think of her family first? Who would you be thinking of in her place?

Rahab lied to protect the spies, and Christians disagree about how to see that. Some say it was right in her situation, others say it was wrong but God honored her faith anyway. How do you weigh a hard moment like this one?
The spies tell her to tie the scarlet cord in the window (v. 18), and she does it right away (v. 21). What does it say about trust that she acted on a promise before anything had happened?
Rahab chose to side with Israel's God over her own city. When, if ever, is it right to break loyalty to your own community because you believe something bigger is at stake?
2.life: Rahab acted on what she had heard about God, even though she had never met his people. This week, think of one person who seems far from God or from church. Do one small, kind thing for them, and pray for them by name.
2.prayer: Thank God that he welcomes people from every background, including the ones others overlook. Ask for the kind of trust Rahab showed, and for eyes to see who around you needs a welcome.
2.tip: Rahab's lie will likely come up, and the group may want a verdict. Say plainly that Christians disagree, then steer back to what the chapter highlights: her faith and her kindness. Also make room for anyone who finds a passage about Israel taking a land uncomfortable, and tell them it is fine to say so.

3.open: What is the most unfamiliar place you have ever had to find your way through, and what helped you get there?
questions: The officers tell the people to follow the ark "since you have never traveled this way before" (v. 4). What is a path in your life right now that you have never traveled before?
The people were told to keep about half a mile behind the ark so they could see the way. What do you think that distance was meant to teach them about God and about following him?
Joshua says, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you" (v. 5). What do you think it meant to get ready, and how do people today prepare themselves to meet with God?
Moses had died, and the people needed to know God was with Joshua too. When a leader or someone you depended on is gone, what helps you trust that God is still with you?

The priests were told to "stand in the Jordan" when they reached the edge of the waters (v. 8). They had to get their feet wet before anything happened. Why do you think God asked for that step first?

The Jordan "overflows its banks throughout the harvest season" (v. 15), so the timing looked impossible. What is something in your life that feels too big or too flooded to cross? You are welcome to say honestly if you are not sure God is in it.
Verse 17 says the priests "stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan" while everyone else crossed. What does it say to you that they stayed in the middle until all the people were through?
Joshua says this will show that "the living God is among you" (v. 10). What helps you recognize God's presence when you cannot see anything dramatic?
3.life: Think of one step you have been putting off because you cannot see how it will turn out. This week, take one small, practical move toward it, and tell someone you trust so they can pray with you.
3.prayer: Thank God that he goes ahead of us on roads we have never traveled. Ask for the courage to take the next step, and pray for anyone in the group who is standing at their own flooded river.
3.tip: Some will want to debate whether the river stopped by a miracle or by a natural event like a landslide that God timed. Name in one line that Christians differ, note that the text itself credits God with the timing and the result, and steer the group back to the question of what it means to trust God with the next step.

4.open: Is there an object in your home, like a photo, a ticket stub or an old tool, that you keep because of the story behind it?
questions: God tells Joshua to choose twelve men, "one from each tribe" (v. 2). Why might it matter that every tribe carried a stone and no one was left out?
The stones were meant to be "a sign among you" (v. 6). Why do you think God chose a pile of stones, something so simple, to hold such a big memory?
The plan depends on children asking, "What do these stones mean to you?" (v. 6). Who first told you the story of your faith, or of your family, and how did they tell it?
The priests kept "standing in the middle of the Jordan" until everyone had crossed (v. 10). Have you ever had to hold your ground in a hard place while others got through? What was that like?
Verse 23 links this crossing to the Red Sea. Why would it help the people to connect what God did then with what God was doing now?
Verse 24 says the stones were so "all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty." How does what God does for one group of people become a witness to others?
Memories fade, even good ones. Is there a time you saw God at work, or hoped you did, that feels distant now? What would you say honestly about it tonight?
If your group built a pile of stones, one for each thing God has done for you, what would you want a child to ask about?
4.life: Choose one story of God's help in your life or family and tell it this week to someone younger, or write it down. Add a small reminder you can see, such as a stone on a windowsill or a note on the fridge.
4.prayer: Thank God for the times he has carried you through, even those you only see looking back. Ask for a good memory and for the courage to pass the story on.
4.tip: Verses 9 and 23 raise questions: how the river stopped, and whether the stones in verse 9 are a second pile. Christians read these differently, some seeing a direct miracle, some seeing God using a natural event, and some seeing a story shaped to teach. Say so in a sentence, then steer back to the point of the chapter: remembering and telling what God has done.

5.open: When did you last get a fresh start, like a new job, a new home or a new school year? What did it feel like?
questions: Verse 1 says the kings' "hearts melted and their spirits failed" when they heard how the LORD had dried up the Jordan. Why do you think a story about a river had that effect on them?

Joshua is told to circumcise a whole generation who had never received the mark of belonging to God's people (vv. 2-7). Why might God want this done now, right before the first battle, and not earlier or later?
The men were then told to stay in camp "until they were healed" (v. 8). What does it say about God's timing that Israel paused to rest and recover before moving on?
God says, "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you" (v. 9). Is there a past shame or label that still follows you around? What would it mean to have it rolled away?
Israel keeps the Passover in the new land, and then the manna stops (vv. 10-12). What is it like when a way God provided for you in one season ends and something different begins?

Joshua asks the armed stranger, "Are You for us or for our enemies?" and hears, "Neither" (vv. 13-14). Why do we so often want God to be on our side? What might it look like to ask whether we are on his?

Joshua "fell facedown in reverence" and was told, "Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy" (vv. 14-15). When have you felt awe, or felt unsure of where you stand before God? Be as honest as you like, including if that feeling is rare for you.

Christians read this figure differently: some see an angel, others see Christ appearing before his birth. Whichever you lean toward, what does this scene tell you about who is really leading the battle?
5.life: Pick one thing from your past that you still carry with shame, or one season that has just ended. This week, tell God about it in plain words and ask him what a fresh start could look like. Then take one small step, such as resting, making a phone call or saying thanks.
5.prayer: Thank God for going ahead of his people and for making new beginnings. Ask him to lift any old shame from you and to help you walk each day on holy ground.
5.tip: Circumcision can feel awkward to talk about in mixed company. Say in one calm sentence that it was the physical sign of belonging to God's covenant, then move on to the bigger point: God gives a fresh start before the work begins. Also, some in the group may feel they have no fresh start to speak of, so let people pass on question 4 without pressure.

6.open: Tell about a time you had to follow instructions that made no sense to you at the time. How did it turn out?
questions: Jericho was "tightly shut up" (v. 1), and God says, "I have delivered Jericho into your hand" (v. 2). Why might it matter that God speaks of the victory as already given before anything has happened?

The plan is to march around the city once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh. What does this plan ask of Joshua and the people, and what would it have felt like to be a soldier in that line?

Joshua tells the people, "do not let one word come out of your mouth until the day I tell you to shout" (v. 10). Why might God ask for silence and waiting? Where in your life are you being asked to wait right now?
The ark and the priests with the horns lead the way, and the army follows. What does that order say about who is really doing the work in this story?

Verse 21 says they devoted "everything in the city" to destruction, including "man and woman, young and old." Many Christians read this very differently, from a one-time act of judgment, to ancient war language, to a picture of the fight against sin, to a partial view of God that Jesus moves beyond. What do you make of it, and what questions does it leave you with? It is fine to say this passage troubles you.

Rahab was spared "because she hid the spies we sent" (v. 17). She was an outsider with a bad reputation, yet she is brought in and lives among Israel. What does her story show about how God treats people others write off?

Verse 18 warns the soldiers to keep away from the things devoted to destruction, and the next chapter shows what happens when someone does not. Why do you think obeying God in the small, private details can be harder than obeying in the big public moments?
The chapter ends with "the LORD was with Joshua" (v. 27). What would it look like for you to trust that God is with you in something where you cannot yet see how it will turn out?
6.life: Pick one situation where you are waiting or feel stuck. Each day this week, take one small, quiet step of obedience or trust in it, and tell God honestly how you feel about the waiting.
6.prayer: Thank God for being faithful to people who seem like outsiders, like Rahab. Ask for patience to wait on him, and for honesty to bring him the parts of the Bible and of life that are hard to understand.
6.tip: Verses 21 and 24 will likely stir strong reactions, and some people may feel uneasy or even angry. Do not rush to defend or explain it away. Name the different ways Christians read it, thank people for being honest, and then turn the group back to what the chapter shows about God's faithfulness, Rahab's rescue and the call to obey.

7.open: Have you ever been part of a group that got in trouble because of one person's choice? What was that like?
questions: Verse 1 says Israel "acted unfaithfully" because of what one man took. Why do you think the text counts one person's secret act as the whole community's problem?
After the defeat, "the hearts of the people melted and became like water" (v. 5). When have you faced a setback that took the courage right out of you?
Joshua says, "why did You ever bring this people across the Jordan" (v. 7). Is it okay to pray with that much frustration and fear? Why or why not?
God answers, "Stand up! Why have you fallen on your face?" (v. 10). What do you hear in that, and how does it change the way you picture God in this scene?

Joshua tells Achan, "do not hide it from me" (v. 19), and Achan says, "I coveted them and took them" (v. 21). His own words show a pattern of seeing, wanting, taking and hiding. Where have you seen that pattern, in the world or in yourself?
The goods were hidden "in the ground inside my tent" (v. 21). What do people tend to bury or hide today, and what does hiding cost them?

The ending is hard to read. Christians disagree about the punishment, especially what happened to Achan's family. How do you honestly respond to this part of the chapter, and what questions does it leave you with?

The valley's name means "trouble" in the story (v. 26), yet later in the Bible the prophets speak of this same valley as a place of hope. What might it mean that God does not leave a place of failure with only its old name?
7.life: This week, set aside ten quiet minutes and ask God whether there is anything you have been hiding or quietly keeping that you should bring into the open. Then tell God, and if it is right, tell one trusted person.
7.prayer: Ask God for honesty about what is hidden in your own life. Thank him that he meets us with a call to stand up and not only with judgment. Pray for anyone in the group carrying a secret or a heavy question.
7.tip: The treatment of Achan's family will likely take over the discussion. Say early that Christians read it differently: some see a one-time act at Israel's beginning, some think the family shared the guilt, and some see old ideas of group guilt that later scripture moves beyond. Let people voice their discomfort without rushing to fix it, then steer back to the chapter's wider themes of hidden sin, honest confession and God's presence.

8.open: Tell about a time you got a second chance at something you had messed up. How did it go?
questions: The LORD begins with "Do not be afraid or discouraged" (v. 1). Joshua had just lost at Ai the first time. What does it say about God that he speaks to a shaken leader this way and sends him back to try again?

Joshua gives careful orders about where to hide, when to rise and what to do next (vv. 4-8). Why do you think God's help here comes through planning and teamwork rather than a miracle like Jericho's walls?

The text says Joshua "spent that night among the people" (v. 9) and later marched at the front with the elders (v. 10). What do you notice about the kind of leader he is, and where have you seen that kind of leadership?

Verse 25 says twelve thousand men and women fell that day, and verse 26 says all who lived in Ai were "devoted to destruction." What stirs in you as you read this? Say it honestly, even if it is discomfort or doubt.

Christians read this kind of passage differently. Some take it as literal history, some as ancient war language that exaggerates, and some read it through the later teaching of Jesus. How do you try to hold a hard passage like this, and what questions does it leave you with?

Right after the destruction, Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and gathers everyone to hear the law (vv. 30-35). Why might Israel stop here to worship and listen to God's word? What do you make of the two scenes sitting side by side?
Verse 35 says Joshua read every word "before the whole assembly of Israel, including the women, the little ones, and the foreigners." Why does it matter that everyone heard it, not just the leaders?
Joshua read both the blessings and the curses (v. 34). How do you feel about hearing God's word when it includes warnings as well as promises? What helps you keep listening?
8.life: Joshua made sure everyone heard God's word. This week, set aside ten minutes on three different days to read a passage out loud, alone or with someone in your home, and notice what stands out when you hear it rather than just read it.
8.prayer: Thank God that he meets us with "Do not be afraid" and gives second chances. Ask him for honesty about the hard parts of Scripture and for a heart that wants to listen to his word.
8.tip: Verses 24 to 26 may be the hardest part of the night, and some people may be troubled or even angry. Do not rush to defend or explain it away. Name the discomfort as fair, say plainly that Christians read the passage in different ways, and let people speak without pressure to reach one answer. Then guide the group back to the whole chapter.

9.open: Have you ever been fooled by something that looked completely real, like a prank, a fake review or a too-good-to-be-true deal?
questions: The Gibeonites planned carefully, with "worn-out sacks," "old wineskins" and "dry and moldy" bread (vv. 4, 5). Why do you think the disguise worked so well on Israel's leaders?
The visitors said they came "because of the fame of the LORD your God" (v. 9). What do you make of the fact that fear of God's power drove them to act this way?
Verse 14 says the men of Israel "sampled their provisions but did not seek the counsel of the LORD." What does it look like today to rely on our own checking and judgment and skip asking God?
When are you most likely to make a quick decision without praying first: money, work, relationships, a big yes or no? What usually pushes you to rush?

Once the truth came out, the leaders said, "We have sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel" (v. 19), and kept their word even though the people grumbled. Why might keeping a promise matter, even when it was made by mistake?
Joshua says to the Gibeonites, "Why did you deceive us?" (v. 22). They answer that they "greatly feared for our lives" (v. 24). How does knowing their reason change the way you see their lie?

Christians read the Gibeonites differently. Some see people who turned toward God and found mercy, and others see deceivers whose trick exposed Israel's carelessness. Which reading seems closer to you, and why?
Think of a time you made a decision you later wished you had slowed down on. What did you learn, and how did you see God at work afterward, or maybe not see him at all?
9.life: Before your next real decision this week, even a small one, stop for a minute and ask God what he would have you do. Then notice whether it changes how you choose.
9.prayer: Ask God for the humility to seek his guidance before acting. Thank him that he is gracious when we get things wrong, and pray for anyone in the group facing a decision right now.
9.tip: The chapter involves a lie, an oath and a people marked for destruction, and some will find it uncomfortable that the deception is rewarded with mercy. Don't rush to tidy it up. Name that Christians read the Gibeonites differently, keep the focus on verse 14 and the keeping of the oath, and let quieter members say what troubles them.

10.open: Tell about a time you were asked for help at a bad moment and showed up anyway.
questions: The men of Gibeon pleaded, "Do not abandon your servants. Come quickly and save us!" (v. 6). Israel had been tricked into this promise in chapter 9, yet Joshua came. What does it say about Joshua that he kept his word? Where is keeping a promise costly for you?
God told Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for I have delivered them into your hand" (v. 8). Then Joshua marched all night (v. 9). How do trusting God and working hard fit together here?
The text says "the LORD threw them into confusion" and sent hailstones (vv. 10, 11). Why do you think the writer wants readers to see God, and not Israel's army, as the one who won?

Verses 12 to 14 describe the sun standing still. Christians read this as a literal miracle, as poetry, or are unsure what the Hebrew means. How do you take it, and does it change what the passage is saying about God?

Joshua tells his commanders to put their feet on the kings' necks and says, "Be strong and courageous, for the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight" (vv. 24, 25). What did that gesture show Israel then? How might we hear courage language differently today?

Verse 40 says Joshua "devoted to destruction everything that breathed, just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded." Christians disagree about how to read this: as literal history, as ancient war language that exaggerates, or as Israel's own picture of God. Where do you find yourself, and what troubles you most about it?
Imagine this chapter told by someone who lived in Lachish or Hebron. What would they notice that we might skip over?
The chapter ends with "the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel" (v. 42). If you are unsure what to make of that today, what would you honestly say to God about it?
10.life: This week, keep one promise you made that has become inconvenient, and when you do, thank God for being faithful when it costs him something. If this chapter's violence has been weighing on you, take that question to God in plain words.
10.prayer: Thank God for being a rescuer who hears the cry of those who call on him. Ask for honesty about the parts of Scripture that trouble us, and for trust to keep asking.
10.tip: Questions 6 and 7 are where people may go quiet or get heated. Say up front that Christians disagree about the destruction of the cities, and that honest questions and unsettled feelings are welcome. Don't rush to resolve it or defend it. Let people stay with the discomfort, and keep coming back to what the chapter says about God's faithfulness and Israel's promise to Gibeon.

11.open: What is something you were told was impossible to do, and then you did it, or watched someone else do it?
questions: The northern kings gathered "a multitude as numerous as the sand on the seashore," with horses and chariots (v. 4). Israel had neither. When have you faced something that felt far bigger than you?
The LORD tells Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them" (v. 6). What do you think made that command possible to obey, and what makes it hard for us?

Joshua was told to hamstring the horses and burn the chariots (v. 6). Many readers see this as a way to keep Israel trusting God rather than weapons. What do you tend to rely on instead of God when things get tense?
Verse 15 says Joshua left "nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses." What does it look like to follow through on obedience, even when it is slow or unglamorous?

The chapter describes whole cities being put to the sword and given over to total destruction (v. 11). What stirs in you as you read that? Say it honestly, whether it is discomfort, confusion or something else.

Verse 20 says it "was of the LORD to harden their hearts." Christians read these commands in different ways: as a unique act of divine judgment, as ancient war language that exaggerates, or as a limited human view of God that later Scripture moves beyond. Which questions does this raise for you about who God is?
Verse 19 notes that the Hivites in Gibeon made peace with Israel. What does that small exception suggest to you?
The chapter ends with "the land had rest from war" (v. 23), though later books show the work was not fully finished. Where are you longing for rest right now, and what would it take to find it?
11.life: Pick one thing this week that feels bigger than you, and name it to God out loud each morning with the words "Do not be afraid" (v. 6). Then ask one trusted person to check in with you on it.
11.prayer: Thank God for being faithful to his promises. Ask for trust when the odds look impossible, and for honesty and humility when the Bible raises questions we cannot answer yet.
11.tip: Verses 11 to 14 and 20 will be the hard spot, and some people may be upset or quiet. Do not rush to defend or explain it away. Say plainly that Christians disagree and that honest questions are welcome, then give people room to speak. If the room stalls, come back to the chapter's themes of fear, trust and rest.

12.open: What is something you keep a list of, like places you have visited, books you have read or jobs you have finished, and why do you keep it?
questions: This chapter is mostly a list. Why do you think the writer stops the story to count up every king? What would be lost if the chapter were skipped?

Verse 1 begins with the kings "whom the Israelites struck down" east of the Jordan, and verse 6 says "Moses, the servant of the LORD" had done this. Why might it matter that Joshua's story counts victories won before him?
Verse 6 says the eastern land was given "as an inheritance" to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. What does it say about God that the land is described as something given and not simply taken?
Og is called "one of the remnant of the Rephaim" (v. 4). Why might the writer remember even the strongest and most feared rulers by name and place?
Verses 9 to 24 repeat "one" after each king, then end with "thirty-one kings in all" (v. 24). What does that steady counting feel like to you as you read it aloud?
Later chapters admit that some of these cities were not fully taken. How do you hold together a record of victory with the honest admission that the work was unfinished?
This chapter describes war and conquest, and Christians read such passages in different ways. What questions or discomfort does it raise for you, and how can we bring those honestly to God?
If you wrote a list of times God has brought you through something, what are one or two things that would be on it, even if some are still unfinished?
12.life: Start a short list this week of ways God has helped you, in your past or in the last month. Add to it each day, and share one item with someone you trust.
12.prayer: Thank God for the ways he has been faithful in the past, including things you may have forgotten. Ask him to help you trust him with the parts of life that still feel unfinished.
12.tip: The violence of the conquest may come up quickly. Say plainly that Christians read this history differently, give people a minute to voice their honest reactions, and then bring the group back to what the chapter does, which is remember and name what God has done. Do not push for one answer.

13.open: What is a project or job you have started but never quite finished? What got in the way?
questions: The LORD says to Joshua, "You are old and well along in years, but very much of the land remains to be possessed" (v. 1). How do you think Joshua felt hearing that? How would you feel?
After years of fighting, large areas were still not under Israel's control (vv. 2-5). Why do you think the Bible is so open about what was left undone?

The LORD says, "I Myself will drive out before the Israelites" the remaining peoples, and then tells Joshua to divide the land anyway (vv. 6-7). What does it look like to act on a promise before you see it fulfilled?
The land was divided "by lot" (v. 6). Why might that have kept the tribes from arguing over who got the best share? Where do we see people quarrelling over fairness today?

Verse 13 says the Israelites "did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites," and they still lived among Israel. Where do you see something unfinished in your own life that you tend to just live with?
Levi received no land. "The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance" (v. 33). What would it be like to have nothing to hold onto except God? What do you tend to hold onto instead?
Joshua is told to hand out land while the work is still unfinished and he will not see it completed. How do you think about passing on something you won't live to finish?
Be honest: when you hear that God makes promises and some things stay unfinished for a long time, what do you feel? Hope, frustration, doubt, something else?
13.life: Think of one person younger than you, or newer to faith, and one practical thing you could hand on to them this week: a story, a skill, a prayer or an hour of your time. Do it without waiting until you feel finished or ready.
13.prayer: Thank God that he keeps working even when we run out of strength or time. Ask him for patience with what is unfinished and for open hands to pass on what he has given you.
13.tip: Most of this chapter is lists of places, and the group may glaze over. Read the two passages aloud but spend your time on verses 1 to 7 and verse 33. If the killings in verses 21 and 22 come up, name them as hard, say honestly that the group does not need to defend or explain them tonight, and move back to the main theme.

14.open: What is the longest you have ever waited for something you were promised or looked forward to?
questions: The land is shared out by a priest, Joshua and a leader from each tribe, and by lot (vv. 1-2). Why might it matter that many people were watching and that no one person chose who got what?
Caleb says he "remained loyal to the LORD my God" when the other spies made the people's hearts "melt with fear" (vv. 8). What do you think it cost him to stand apart from the majority?
Moses said Caleb had "wholly followed the LORD" (v. 9). What do you think it looks like to follow God wholeheartedly in ordinary life, not just in big moments?
Caleb waited forty five years between the promise and the day he asked for it. What helps you keep trusting when an answer takes much longer than you hoped?

Caleb says he is "still as strong today" as when Moses sent him out (v. 11). He sees his long life as God keeping him alive, as the LORD promised (v. 10). Where do you see God's care in your own years, even if it is hard to see right now?

Caleb asks for "this hill country," where the Anakim lived in "great and fortified cities" (v. 12). Why do you think he picked the hardest ground, and what is a hard thing you might ask God's help with?

Caleb says, "Perhaps with the LORD's help I will drive them out" (v. 12). He sounds hopeful but not cocksure. Where do you land today: confident, unsure, or somewhere in between? Say it as honestly as you can.

This land was taken from people who already lived there, and later chapters show the story was not tidy. How do we read a chapter like this with both gratitude for God's promise and honesty about its hard side?
14.life: Think of one promise from God, or one hope you have carried for a long time. This week, write it down and tell one person in the group how you are holding onto it, or how hard that has been.
14.prayer: Thank God for being faithful across long years. Ask for steady trust while you wait, and for the courage to take on the hard thing in front of you.
14.tip: The last question touches the conquest, which troubles many people. Do not rush to defend or dismiss it. Name it plainly, let people say what bothers them, and bring the group back to Caleb's faithfulness and the chapter's central point.

15.open: Think of a place you have lived or visited. What is one thing about it that you would want a newcomer to know before moving there?
questions: Most of this chapter is boundaries and town names. Why might God's people have wanted all of that written down, and what does it say about how God cares for ordinary, practical things?

Verse 13 says Joshua gave Caleb his portion "according to the LORD's command to him." Caleb received something that had been promised to him. When have you seen a promise take a long time to be kept, and how did waiting feel?
Caleb "drove out" the three sons of Anak (v. 14), a people remembered as huge and strong. What is the Anak in your life right now, the thing that feels too big to face?

Caleb offers his daughter to whoever captures Kiriath-sepher (v. 16). That was a way of honoring bravery in that culture, and it can sound strange to us. What questions or discomfort does it raise for you, and how do you read it?

Acsah says, "Give me a blessing," and asks for "springs of water as well" (v. 19). She already had land, but dry land is hard to live on. What are you asking God or others for that would make what you already have livable?

Acsah asked her father plainly, and he gave her "both the upper and lower springs" (v. 19). What makes it easy or hard for you to ask God for something directly? If you are unsure he listens, you can say so.

Verse 63 says Judah "could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem." The land was given, yet not all of it was taken. Where do you see a gap between what God has promised and what you actually experience?
Why do you think the writer admitted that failure instead of leaving it out? What does honesty about unfinished business make possible for a person or a community?
15.life: Acsah asked for what would make her land livable. This week, name one practical need or dry spot in your life and ask God for it plainly, once a day. Then tell one person in the group what you asked.
15.prayer: Thank God for keeping his promises, even slowly. Ask him for the "springs" each person in the group needs, and for honesty about what is still unfinished.
15.tip: The long list of towns can lose people. Don't read it aloud in full. Read the borders briefly, spend most of the time on Caleb and Acsah, and treat the list as a sign that the land was real and each place mattered. Verse 16 may bother some people, so let them say so, and note that it reflects the customs of the time rather than a model to copy.

16.open: Think about a place you have lived or a home you have loved. What made it feel like yours?
questions: Most of this chapter is a list of borders and place names. Why might the writer have thought it was worth keeping, and what does it tell you about how the Bible treats real places and real people?
Verse 4 says, "Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, received their inheritance." The word is received, not earned. What do you have that you did not earn but simply received?
Ephraim and Manasseh were descended from brothers, and some of Ephraim's towns sat inside Manasseh's land (v. 9). What does it take for relatives or neighbors to share space well?
Ephraim's section gives borders but no list of towns, and nobody knows for sure why. How do you feel about passages that leave questions like that unanswered?
Verse 10 says, "they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer." The writer reports this plainly and does not soften it. Why might Scripture be honest about its own people's failures?

The Canaanites of Gezer became "forced laborers" (v. 10). The text states this without comment. How does it sit with you, and what do you think those who settle a land owe the people already living there?
Ephraim left a job half done and lived with it for generations. Where in your own life have you left something unfinished or settled for less than you were asked to do?
If you are not sure what to make of a chapter like this, or of how God is described in the land stories, what would you honestly like to ask or say?
16.life: Pick one half-finished thing you have been putting off, such as a conversation, a repair, or a habit. Take one small step on it this week, and tell God or a friend where you are stuck.
16.prayer: Thank God for the gifts you received and did not earn. Ask for honesty about what you have left undone, and for care toward the people who live alongside you.
16.tip: Verse 10 can lead quickly into hard questions about conquest and the Canaanites. Name that the question is real, note that the chapter itself only reports it plainly, and keep the group on what it shows about honesty and unfinished obedience. Invite anyone who wants to go deeper to keep talking after the meeting.

17.open: What is something you ever had to ask for, even though you were nervous to ask?
questions: Zelophehad "had no sons but only daughters" (v. 3). In that world, land normally passed through sons. What risk were these five women taking when they came forward?

The daughters said, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers" (v. 4). Why do you think they spoke up with something God had already said, rather than just asking for a favor?
Joshua gave them land "in keeping with the command of the LORD" (v. 4). What does it show about the leaders that they honored this promise, even though it was inconvenient?

Verse 12 says the descendants of Manasseh could not take these cities because the Canaanites were set on staying in the land. Where do you feel up against something that will not budge, in your life or in the world?

Verse 13 says that when Israel grew stronger, they used the Canaanites for forced labor but "failed to drive them out completely." What do you think it looks like to take an easier path than the one we were asked to take?
The sons of Joseph complained, "Why have you given us only one portion?" (v. 14). When is it fair to ask for more, and when is it just a way of avoiding hard work?

Joshua answers, "Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can drive them out" (v. 18). Is there something you believe is too big for you right now? What would it take to hear this as encouragement rather than pressure?
Be honest: when you read a chapter full of land borders and long delays, where do you find it hard to see God in it, and what, if anything, stands out to you?
17.life: Think of one thing you have been waiting for someone else to fix or approve. This week, take one small, honest step toward it, whether that is asking a question, making a call or beginning the work.
17.prayer: Thank God that he sees people the usual rules overlook, like these five sisters. Ask for courage to speak up when something is right, and for the willingness to finish what he has given you to do.
17.tip: This chapter has a lot of place names and borders, so do not try to cover them. Spend your time on the sisters in verses 3 to 6 and on Joshua's reply in verses 14 to 18. Question 8 gives people a way to say the chapter feels dry, so welcome that honestly.

18.open: What is something you kept putting off for a long time, and what finally got you to do it?
questions: The people "set up the Tent of Meeting there" at Shiloh before the land was divided (v. 1). Why might it matter that worship was set in the middle first? What sits at the center of your week right now?

Seven tribes "had not yet received their inheritance" even though the land was already won (vv. 1-2). Joshua asks, "How long will you put off entering and possessing the land" (v. 3). Why do people hold back from something already within reach? The text does not say why they waited, so what do you think?
Is there something good you have held back from, maybe out of tiredness, fear or doubt? Be as honest as you like about what makes it hard to step in.

Joshua asks each tribe to send three men to "survey the land and map it out" (v. 4). What do you notice about sharing the work and writing it all down? What does that say about how God works through ordinary planning?

Joshua says, "I will cast lots for you here in the presence of the LORD our God" (v. 6). What is it like to let go of choosing your own portion? Where do you find it hard to accept what you have been given?

The Levites had no land, because "their inheritance is the priesthood of the LORD" (v. 7). What does it mean that their share was not a region on the map? What do you count as your inheritance, and is it always something you can see?
Benjamin's land lay "between the tribes of Judah and Joseph" (v. 11), a small strip next to two big tribes. How do you feel about comparing your share to someone else's, and what helps?
18.life: Think of one thing you have been putting off that is already within reach, such as a call, a conversation, a habit or a step of faith. This week take one small, specific step toward it, and tell someone in the group what it was.
18.prayer: Thank God for the inheritance he has given, seen and unseen. Ask for honesty about what holds us back, and for the courage to take the next small step.
18.tip: The long lists of borders and towns can make eyes glaze over. Read them aloud briefly or skim them, and point out that the detail shows each tribe's share was real and fairly recorded. Spend your time on verses 1 to 10, and be careful not to claim you know why the seven tribes waited, since the text does not say.

19.open: Where did you grow up, and what is one thing about that place you still miss or still remember?
questions: Most of this chapter is lists of towns and borders. Why do you think the writer kept all these names instead of summing it up in a sentence? What does it say about how God treats ordinary places and people?
Verse 9 says Simeon's share was taken from Judah's portion, because Judah's land was "too large for them." What do you notice about Judah giving up part of what it had received?

Each tribe's land came by lot, and verse 51 says this happened "before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting." How do you feel about the idea that your place in life could be something given to you rather than something you earned or chose?

Verse 47 says the Danites lost their territory and went north to take Leshem. What does it look like when people settle for a different place than the one they were given? Where have you seen that, in the Bible or in life?
The people gave Joshua his town only after every tribe was settled (v. 49). Why might it matter that he went last? What does it show about the kind of leader he was?
Verse 50 says Joshua "rebuilt the city and settled in it." What do you think it means to take what you are given and make a home of it, even when it is not perfect?
Some of us feel settled and at home, and some of us feel like we are still waiting for our own place. Where are you right now, and what would you honestly say to God about it?
Verse 51 says "they finished dividing up the land." What is something in your life that took a long time to finish, and how did it feel to reach the end?
19.life: Choose one person this week who is waiting for something, such as a job, a home, a friendship or an answer. Put their needs ahead of your own in one practical way, like a meal, a call or an hour of your time.
19.prayer: Thank God that he knows each person by name and gives each one a place. Ask him to help the group be content where they are, and to be generous toward those who are still waiting.
19.tip: The long list of place names can make people tune out. Do not read every name aloud. Read the two suggested sections, point out a few moments that stand out (Simeon inside Judah, Dan moving north, Joshua going last), and move quickly to the questions.

20.open: Have you ever had a place that felt like a safe harbor when things went wrong, like a friend's kitchen table or a quiet spot you could go?
questions: God says these cities are for someone who "kills another unintentionally or accidentally" (v. 3). Why do you think God cared about the difference between an accident and a deliberate act?

In that culture a relative, called the avenger of blood, was expected to take a life in return. What was the danger these cities were meant to stop, and what does that tell us about how God sees justice?
The person had to stand at the city gate and state "his case before its elders" (v. 4). Why might it matter that the story was heard before anyone decided anything?

The elders were told to "give him a place to live among them" (v. 4). What would it have cost a town to take in someone people were angry at? When have you seen a community make room for someone in trouble?

The person stayed until "he stands trial before the assembly" and until the high priest died (v. 6). Scholars are not sure why the high priest's death mattered. What do you think a fresh start would have felt like after that long wait?
These cities were open to "all the Israelites and foreigners among them" (v. 9). Who might feel like an outsider where you live or in our church, and how could we make safety plainly open to them?

Even an accidental harm leaves a mark on the person who caused it and on the family who lost someone. If you are comfortable, share a time you felt guilt or fear, whether deserved or not, and what helped. It is fine to say you are not sure God feels like a refuge right now.

Some Christians read these cities as a picture of finding safety in Jesus, and others see them mainly as a practical justice law for ancient Israel. Whichever you lean toward, what does this chapter show you about the kind of God who set them up?
20.life: Think of one person who feels shut out, blamed or alone, whether rightly or not. This week, give them your time: a call, a meal or simply listening to their side before forming an opinion.
20.prayer: Thank God that he cares about fairness and mercy together. Ask him to be a safe place for anyone in the group carrying guilt or fear, and to make us a people who make room for others.
20.tip: Questions 5 and 7 can pull the group into debating whether the high priest detail has a hidden meaning or into personal guilt. Say plainly that scholars are unsure about the high priest, then keep the focus on mercy and a fair hearing. Let people pass on question 7 without pressure.

21.open: Think of a place you have lived that felt like home. What made it feel that way?
questions: The Levite leaders came forward and reminded Joshua of what God had already said: "The LORD commanded through Moses that we be given cities in which to live" (v. 2). Why might it take courage to ask for something you were promised?
The other tribes gave these towns "out of their own inheritance" (v. 3). What did it cost them, and what does it say about how God's people are meant to treat those who serve them?
Lots were drawn to decide where each Levite family would live (v. 4). What is it like to hand a big decision over to God instead of choosing for yourself? Where do you find that hard?
The Levites were spread through every tribe instead of living in one block. Why might God want people who teach and lead worship living among everyone else? Who has played that role in your life?
Hebron went to the priests, but the fields around it stayed with Caleb (vv. 11 and 12). What does that small detail suggest about how God keeps earlier promises while making new ones?
Verse 44 says "the LORD gave them rest on every side." What does rest look like in your life right now, and what is getting in its way?

Verse 45 says, "Not one of all the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel had failed." Some of us read that and feel hopeful, and some feel unsure, because not every promise seems kept in our own lives. Where are you honestly at with that today?

Earlier chapters mention peoples who were never fully driven out, and Gezer, listed here, is one of them. How do you hold together a big claim that God kept his word with the messiness still left over?
21.life: Think of someone who serves your church or community, such as a pastor, a teacher, a volunteer or a caregiver, and who may rarely be thanked. This week, give them something practical: a meal, a note, or an offer to take a task off their hands.
21.prayer: Thank God for being faithful to what he has said. Ask him for patience with the promises you are still waiting on, and for open hands toward the people who serve you.
21.tip: Verses 43 to 45 can raise a fair question: if every promise was kept, why do other chapters say some enemies remained? Don't rush to smooth it over. Name the tension, mention that Christians differ on whether this rest was complete in Joshua's day or pointed ahead to a deeper rest, and let people stay with the question. Also, don't let the long list of town names drag. Read the first and last sections aloud and summarize the middle in a sentence.

22.open: Tell about a time you were sure you knew why someone did something, and it turned out you were wrong.
questions: Joshua tells the eastern tribes, "You have done all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you" (v. 2). Why might it matter that he praises them before he sends them home? Who in your life could use that kind of recognition?

Joshua's charge is "to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to keep His commandments, to hold fast to Him, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul" (v. 5). Which of those phrases feels easiest to you right now, and which feels hardest?
When the report arrived, "the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh to go to war against them" (v. 12). What do you think drove them to act so fast? Why do we so often react before we ask?

The leaders pointed to Peor and Achan, times when one group's sin hurt everyone (vv. 17, 20). Their fear was real, and they also offered to share their own land (v. 19). What do you notice about how they handled it, both the good and the heavy-handed?

The eastern tribes answered, "The LORD, the Mighty One, is God!" and then explained their fear that their children would be told, "You have no share in the LORD!" (vv. 22, 25). Have you ever worried that you or your family might be seen as outsiders in a faith community? What was that like?
Phinehas listened and said, "Today we know that the LORD is among us" (v. 31). What does it take for us to listen to someone's explanation when we are already upset? What helps you do it?

The altar was named Witness, "a witness between us that the LORD is God" (v. 34). What reminders do you or your family keep, such as objects, traditions or places, that point you and the next generation back to God?
If you feel unsure or distant when you hear a call to love God with everything you have, as in verse 5, what would you honestly say is going on for you right now?
22.life: This week, when you catch yourself assuming the worst about someone, stop and ask them a direct, kind question before you decide what they meant. Then notice what you learn.
22.prayer: Thank God for the people who stand with us across distance and difference. Ask for patience to listen before judging, and for a heart that keeps hold of him.
22.tip: The leaders' threat of war and their talk of punishing the whole nation can feel harsh, and some people may side with the eastern tribes while others defend the leaders. Rather than ruling on who was right, point the group to how the chapter ends: they talked first, and peace followed.

23.open: Who is someone older than you whose advice you still remember, and what did they tell you?
questions: Joshua says, "it was the LORD your God who fought for you" (v. 3). Why do you think he gives God the credit instead of himself or the army?
Joshua tells them to "hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day" (v. 8). What does holding fast to God look like in an ordinary week, not just on Sunday?

Verse 10 says "One of you can put a thousand to flight, because the LORD your God fights for you." Think of a time when something was bigger than your own strength. Where did your help come from, or did it feel like none came?
Joshua sums up his whole message with "watch yourselves carefully, that you love the LORD your God" (v. 11). Why might he say love, and not just obey? How are they different?

In verses 12 and 13 Joshua warns about mixing in with the nations that remain, and says they will become "a snare and a trap." Back then this was about serving other gods. What small compromises today can slowly pull a person's heart away from God?

Verse 14 says "not one of the good promises the LORD your God made to you has failed." Is that easy or hard for you to say about your own life right now? Be as honest as you like, including if you have doubts.
Verses 15 and 16 say that God's warnings are as sure as his promises. How do you hold together a God who is faithful and generous with a God who takes unfaithfulness seriously?
Joshua is old and knows his time is short, and he spends it on what matters most. If you had one chance to speak to the next generation, what would you want to tell them?
23.life: Joshua points back to what God has already done as a reason to stay loyal. This week, write down three things God has brought you through or given you, and read the list aloud once before you go to bed.
23.prayer: Thank God for being faithful to his promises. Ask him to help each person in the group love him with their whole heart and stay close to him.
23.tip: Verses 12 to 16 can sound harsh, and some people will hear them as a threat. Keep the focus on Joshua's reason in verse 14: God has been faithful, so Israel's loyalty is a response to that. Also be careful with the talk of intermarriage and nations. The concern in the text is about worshipping other gods, not about any people being lesser, so steer the group back to that if the talk drifts.

24.open: Think of a promise you made that turned out to be harder to keep than you expected. What happened?
questions: Joshua starts the story with Abraham's family, who "worshiped other gods" (v. 2). Why might he begin there, with where they came from, before talking about what they should do?
In verse 13 God says, "I gave you a land on which you did not toil and cities that you did not build." What do you have today that you did not earn or build yourself?
Joshua says, "choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve" (v. 15). What are some of the "gods" people around us serve today, and which ones quietly pull at you?
Joshua says, "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" (v. 15). What would that look like in your home, your friendships or your daily routine, whatever your situation is?

The people promise loyalty, and Joshua answers, "You are not able to serve the LORD" (v. 19). Many readers see this as a jolt meant to make them think before they promise. Why might someone say that to people who are so eager?
Joshua tells them to "get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD" (v. 23). Why does he ask for both an action and a change of heart? Which one is harder for you?
Joshua sets up a stone as a witness (vv. 26-27). What reminders, people or habits help you remember what you have committed to?

Be honest here. Is there part of this chapter, the strong promises, the warning about a holy and jealous God, or the call to choose, that you find hard to take in right now? Where do you find yourself in it?
24.life: Joshua rooted a present choice in remembered history. This week, write down three things God has done for you or your family. Read them over once a day, and then tell one person about one of them.
24.prayer: Thank God for what he has done in your story, including gifts you did not earn. Ask him to show you anything that competes with him for your heart, and for help to follow him with sincerity.
24.tip: Verses 19 and 20 can feel harsh, and people may ask why Joshua discourages them. Do not rush to explain it away. Point out that the people hear the warning and still choose, and invite the group to say what they notice. Keep the tone gentle so that quieter members feel free to be honest.
